NONPROFIT RELIGIOUS CORPORATION — FORMATION INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Acme Fellowship

NONPROFIT RELIGIOUS CORPORATION PURPOSE AND AGENT DECLARATION
The name of the corporation is Acme Fellowship. Acme Fellowship is a religious corporation and is not organized for the private gain of any person. It is organized under the Nonprofit Religious Corporation Law the advancement of religious worship and education for religious purposes. and to operate a religious school The initial street address of Acme Fellowship is 500 Market St, San Francisco, CA 94105. The name of Acme Fellowship's initial agent for service of process in California is Jordan Alex Lee. The agent's street address in California is 500 Market St, San Francisco, CA 94105.

REQUIRED CONTENT OF NONPROFIT RELIGIOUS CORPORATION ARTICLES
California's Nonprofit Religious Corporation Law contains its own required-content statute for a religious corporation's articles of incorporation, separate from the required-content statutes that govern a nonprofit public benefit corporation and a nonprofit mutual benefit corporation. The religious-corporation statute requires the filed articles to state: the corporation's name; a specific, statutorily prescribed statement that the corporation “is a religious corporation and is not organized for the private gain of any person” and is organized under the Nonprofit Religious Corporation Law “(primarily or exclusively [insert one or both])” for religious purposes, with a further description of the corporation's purpose always optional and never mandatory; the name and California street address of the corporation's initial agent for service of process; the corporation's initial street address; and its initial mailing address, if that differs from the street address. Two features distinguish this required-content list from the nonprofit public benefit corporation's: first, the prescribed statement does not offer a choice between two different kinds of purpose (“public” or “charitable,” as the public benefit statute does) but instead asks only how exclusively religious the corporation's purpose is (“primarily”, “exclusively”, or both); second, a further description of purpose is optional in every case for a religious corporation, where the public benefit statute makes a further description mandatory whenever “public” purposes are elected. Third, and more a structural quirk than a substantive difference, the religious-corporation statute's agent-for-service-of-process requirement is not itself a direct grant of the general corporation law's agent statute; it cross-references “Section 6210 (made applicable pursuant to Section 9660)” — the same underlying agent-designation rule public and mutual benefit corporations use, but adopted into the religious corporation law by a separate incorporating statute rather than cited directly. As with the other two nonprofit corporation types, nothing in this list calls for a statement of authorized shares — a nonprofit religious corporation has no shareholders and issues no stock.

  — Cal. Corp. Code § 9130(a)-(b), California Nonprofit Religious Corporation Law, the required name and statutory purpose statement (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=9130.)
  "“This corporation is a religious corporation and is not organized for the private gain of any person. It is organized under the Nonprofit Religious Corporation Law (primarily or exclusively [insert one or both]) for religious purposes.”"

(d) The initial street address of the corporation. (e) The initial mailing address of the corporation, if different from the initial street address."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 9130(c)-(e), California Nonprofit Religious Corporation Law, agent for service of process and required addresses (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=9130.)

ELIGIBILITY STANDARD: “PRIMARILY OR EXCLUSIVELY... RELIGIOUS PURPOSES”
California's Nonprofit Corporation Law sets a genuinely different eligibility standard for a religious corporation than it sets for a nonprofit public benefit corporation, and each standard appears in its own dedicated “Title and Purposes” article at the head of the respective part of the statute. The religious-corporation statute provides that, subject to other law applying to a particular class of corporation or line of activity, “a corporation may be formed under this part primarily or exclusively for any religious purposes.” The nonprofit public benefit statute uses the identical opening structure but a different substantive standard: “a corporation may be formed under this part for any public or charitable purposes.” The two standards are not the same text with different labels substituted in — the religious-corporation statute alone builds in the “primarily or exclusively” qualifier that describes how completely religious the corporation's purposes must be, and that qualifier is what the required purpose statement in the corporation's articles (covered above) later asks the incorporator to elect between. A corporation eligible to form under the religious-corporation statute is accordingly one formed primarily or exclusively for religious purposes — not, as with a public benefit corporation, one formed for public or charitable purposes more broadly, of which a religious purpose could be only one example.

  — Cal. Corp. Code § 9111, California Nonprofit Religious Corporation Law, the formation-eligibility standard (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=9111.)
  "Subject to any other provisions of law of this state applying to the particular class of corporation or line of activity, a corporation may be formed under this part for any public or charitable purposes."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 5111, California Nonprofit Public Benefit Corporation Law, the formation-eligibility standard, for contrast (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=5111.)

REDUCED ATTORNEY GENERAL OVERSIGHT OF RELIGIOUS CORPORATIONS
California law imposes a specific, statute-based limit on the Attorney General's power over an entity “incorporated or classified as a religious corporation” that has no equivalent stated so broadly for a nonprofit public benefit corporation. The religious-corporation statute provides that, apart from the Attorney General's ordinary criminal-law-enforcement role, “the Attorney General shall have no powers with respect to any corporation incorporated or classified as a religious corporation under or pursuant to this code” except as expressly granted by three narrow, listed carve-outs: authority to bring a declaratory-relief action to determine that an entity is not properly qualified or classified as a religious corporation in the first place; the specific authority separately granted over the religious-corporation law's own filing, sale-of-assets, merger, and dissolution provisions (covered elsewhere in this document); the ordinary authority to prosecute crimes; authority to represent other state agencies with their own express authority over religious corporations; and a narrow authority to sue only where property was solicited from the general public for a specific charitable purpose and then diverted from that purpose. A separate statute confirms the same reduced role from another angle: the Attorney General's Registry of Charitable Trusts filing, registration, and reporting regime — the ongoing state charity-oversight filings that apply generally to entities holding charitable assets — by its own terms “do[es] not apply to... any religious corporation sole or other religious corporation or organization that holds property for religious purposes,” a categorical exemption not extended in that same provision to a nonprofit public benefit corporation generally (the statute separately exempts only certain other categories, such as an educational institution, a hospital, or a charitable organization “organized and operated primarily as a religious organization” — an ordinary public benefit charity outside those categories remains subject to the filing and reporting regime). This combination — a narrow, enumerated list of the Attorney General's powers over religious corporations specifically, plus a separate exemption from the ongoing charitable-registry filings — is commonly discussed as reflecting First Amendment church-autonomy concerns, though the statutory text itself does not state that rationale; this document reports what the statutes say, not why the Legislature enacted them.

  — Cal. Corp. Code § 9230(a), California Nonprofit Religious Corporation Law, the general bar on Attorney General powers (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=9230.)
  "The Attorney General shall have authority to institute an action or proceeding under Section 803 of the Code of Civil Procedure, to obtain judicial determination that a corporation is not properly qualified or classified as a religious corporation under the provisions of this part."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 9230(b), California Nonprofit Religious Corporation Law, the narrow declaratory-relief carve-out (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=9230.)

THE NO-DISTRIBUTIONS RULE APPLIES BY CROSS-REFERENCE, WITH A NARROWER ENFORCEMENT LIST
Unlike a nonprofit public benefit corporation and a nonprofit mutual benefit corporation, each of which has its own freestanding “Distributions” chapter stating the no-distribution rule in its own words, the Nonprofit Religious Corporation Law does not restate that rule at all — it adopts the public benefit corporation's distributions chapter by cross-reference instead. The religious corporation statute provides: “The provisions of Chapter 4 (commencing with Section 5410) of Part 2 apply to religious corporations except for subdivision (b) of Section 5420.” Chapter 4 of Part 2 is the same public benefit corporation distributions chapter already covered elsewhere in this project's public benefit corporation document, whose central rule is: “No corporation shall make any distribution,” subject to a narrow carve-out for limited-equity housing cooperative memberships. Because the religious-corporation statute imports that rule by reference rather than granting an outright exemption from it, a religious corporation is, on this point, subject to essentially the same substantive no-distributions rule as a public benefit corporation. The one piece the cross-reference deliberately excludes — subdivision (b) of Section 5420, the public benefit statute's own provision on who may sue over a wrongful distribution — is replaced with the religious corporation law's own, narrower version, and the difference between the two lists is specific: the public benefit provision states that “suit may be brought in the name of a corporation by a creditor, a director, the Attorney General, or... a member,” while the religious corporation's own replacement provision states that “suit may be brought in the name of the corporation by a creditor, a director, or the authorized number of members” — omitting the Attorney General from the list of people who may sue to enforce the no-distributions rule against a religious corporation, a further, specific instance of the reduced Attorney General enforcement role addressed in the clause above.

DISSOLUTION: ASSETS DISPOSED OF UNDER THE CORPORATION'S OWN ARTICLES, WITH A WEAKER ATTORNEY GENERAL ROLE
California's dissolution statutes give a religious corporation a genuinely different, and lighter, Attorney General role in the final disposition of its assets than the role a nonprofit public benefit corporation faces. The religious-corporation statute again proceeds by cross-reference and exclusion: it provides that the public benefit corporation law's winding-up and dissolution chapters “apply to religious corporations except for Sections 6610, 6614, 6710, 6711 and 6716” — an express carve-out of Section 6716, which is the public benefit corporation's own asset-disposition statute (already covered in this project's public benefit corporation document). In its place, the religious corporation statute supplies its own, separately worded disposition rule: assets are disposed of “in conformity with its articles or bylaws subject to complying with the provisions of any trust under which such assets are held,” and that disposition “shall be made by decree of the superior court of the proper county. The decree shall be made upon petition therefor, upon 30 days' notice to the Attorney General, by any person concerned in the dissolution.” The excluded public benefit statute, by contrast, requires that the disposition “be made by decree of the superior court of the proper county in proceedings to which the Attorney General is a party.” The substance of the two rules is otherwise close — both look first to the corporation's own articles or bylaws, both route the actual disposition through a superior court decree, and both give the Attorney General a role — but the religious-corporation version's role for the Attorney General is notice and an opportunity to object, not formal party status in the court proceeding itself, which is exactly what the excluded public benefit statute requires.

GOVERNANCE FLEXIBILITY: ARTICLES OR BYLAWS MAY OVERRIDE THE MEMBERS' STATUTORY REMOVAL POWER
California's default rule letting members remove a director without cause is worded differently, and is more freely displaceable, for a religious corporation than the corresponding default rule is for either a nonprofit public benefit corporation or a nonprofit mutual benefit corporation. The religious-corporation statute provides: “Except as provided in the articles or bylaws and subject to subdivision (b) of this section, any or all directors may be removed without cause if the removal is approved by the members.” The opening qualifier — “Except as provided in the articles or bylaws” — gives a religious corporation's own governing documents a general power to displace or modify this default in whatever way they choose. The corresponding public benefit corporation statute states the same basic default — members may remove a director without cause — but opens instead with “Subject to subdivisions (b) and (f) of this section,” not with any general “except as provided in the articles or bylaws” carve-out; its only built-in flexibility is the specific cumulative-voting protection in subdivision (b) and the specific designator-consent mechanism in subdivision (f), not a general license for the articles or bylaws to override the members' removal power itself. The nonprofit mutual benefit corporation's parallel removal statute is worded the same restrictive way as the public benefit corporation's. On this specific point — whether the corporation's own articles or bylaws may override the members' statutory power to remove a director without cause — the religious-corporation statute is the only one of the three that says so in its own opening text.

FEDERAL TAX-EXEMPT STATUS REMAINS A SEPARATE QUESTION, WHERE “RELIGIOUS” IS ITSELF A LISTED IRC PURPOSE
The same point already made in this project's Nonprofit Public Benefit Corporation and Nonprofit Mutual Benefit Corporation documents applies here without needing to be re-derived: California's formation statute for a religious corporation — including the required purpose statement covered above — governs only what must appear in the articles filed with the California Secretary of State, and does not itself confer, guarantee, or evaluate federal tax-exempt status, which is a separate determination made by the Internal Revenue Service under federal law. One detail is specific to a religious corporation, however: the federal statute those other two documents already identify as the source of the 501(c)(3) organizational test lists “religious” purposes by name, on equal footing with “charitable,” “scientific,” and “educational” purposes, as one of the purposes for which a corporation must be “organized and operated exclusively” to qualify for exemption under 26 U.S.C. § 501(c)(3). That federal statutory alignment between the word “religious” in California's own formation statute and the word “religious” in the federal exemption statute does not collapse the two determinations into one — satisfying California's state-law purpose statement is still not the same thing as satisfying the IRS's separate organizational and operational tests under federal law, for the same reasons already given in this project's other two nonprofit corporation documents.

expectedJSON.body: California law imposes a specific, statute-based limit on the Attorney General's power over an entity “incorporated or classified as a religious corporation” that has no equivalent stated so broadly for a nonprofit public benefit corporation. The religious-corporation statute provides that, apart from the Attorney General's ordinary criminal-law-enforcement role, “the Attorney General shall have no powers with respect to any corporation incorporated or classified as a religious corporation under or pursuant to this code” except as expressly granted by three narrow, listed carve-outs: authority to bring a declaratory-relief action to determine that an entity is not properly qualified or classified as a religious corporation in the first place; the specific authority separately granted over the religious-corporation law's own filing, sale-of-assets, merger, and dissolution provisions (covered elsewhere in this document); the ordinary authority to prosecute crimes; authority to represent other state agencies with their own express authority over religious corporations; and a narrow authority to sue only where property was solicited from the general public for a specific charitable purpose and then diverted from that purpose. A separate statute confirms the same reduced role from another angle: the Attorney General's Registry of Charitable Trusts filing, registration, and reporting regime — the ongoing state charity-oversight filings that apply generally to entities holding charitable assets — by its own terms “do[es] not apply to... any religious corporation sole or other religious corporation or organization that holds property for religious purposes,” a categorical exemption not extended in that same provision to a nonprofit public benefit corporation generally (the statute separately exempts only certain other categories, such as an educational institution, a hospital, or a charitable organization “organized and operated primarily as a religious organization” — an ordinary public benefit charity outside those categories remains subject to the filing and reporting regime). This combination — a narrow, enumerated list of the Attorney General's powers over religious corporations specifically, plus a separate exemption from the ongoing charitable-registry filings — is commonly discussed as reflecting First Amendment church-autonomy concerns, though the statutory text itself does not state that rationale; this document reports what the statutes say, not why the Legislature enacted them.

expectedJSON.body: Unlike a nonprofit public benefit corporation and a nonprofit mutual benefit corporation, each of which has its own freestanding “Distributions” chapter stating the no-distribution rule in its own words, the Nonprofit Religious Corporation Law does not restate that rule at all — it adopts the public benefit corporation's distributions chapter by cross-reference instead. The religious corporation statute provides: “The provisions of Chapter 4 (commencing with Section 5410) of Part 2 apply to religious corporations except for subdivision (b) of Section 5420.” Chapter 4 of Part 2 is the same public benefit corporation distributions chapter already covered elsewhere in this project's public benefit corporation document, whose central rule is: “No corporation shall make any distribution,” subject to a narrow carve-out for limited-equity housing cooperative memberships. Because the religious-corporation statute imports that rule by reference rather than granting an outright exemption from it, a religious corporation is, on this point, subject to essentially the same substantive no-distributions rule as a public benefit corporation. The one piece the cross-reference deliberately excludes — subdivision (b) of Section 5420, the public benefit statute's own provision on who may sue over a wrongful distribution — is replaced with the religious corporation law's own, narrower version, and the difference between the two lists is specific: the public benefit provision states that “suit may be brought in the name of a corporation by a creditor, a director, the Attorney General, or... a member,” while the religious corporation's own replacement provision states that “suit may be brought in the name of the corporation by a creditor, a director, or the authorized number of members” — omitting the Attorney General from the list of people who may sue to enforce the no-distributions rule against a religious corporation, a further, specific instance of the reduced Attorney General enforcement role addressed in the clause above.

expectedJSON.body: California's dissolution statutes give a religious corporation a genuinely different, and lighter, Attorney General role in the final disposition of its assets than the role a nonprofit public benefit corporation faces. The religious-corporation statute again proceeds by cross-reference and exclusion: it provides that the public benefit corporation law's winding-up and dissolution chapters “apply to religious corporations except for Sections 6610, 6614, 6710, 6711 and 6716” — an express carve-out of Section 6716, which is the public benefit corporation's own asset-disposition statute (already covered in this project's public benefit corporation document). In its place, the religious corporation statute supplies its own, separately worded disposition rule: assets are disposed of “in conformity with its articles or bylaws subject to complying with the provisions of any trust under which such assets are held,” and that disposition “shall be made by decree of the superior court of the proper county. The decree shall be made upon petition therefor, upon 30 days' notice to the Attorney General, by any person concerned in the dissolution.” The excluded public benefit statute, by contrast, requires that the disposition “be made by decree of the superior court of the proper county in proceedings to which the Attorney General is a party.” The substance of the two rules is otherwise close — both look first to the corporation's own articles or bylaws, both route the actual disposition through a superior court decree, and both give the Attorney General a role — but the religious-corporation version's role for the Attorney General is notice and an opportunity to object, not formal party status in the court proceeding itself, which is exactly what the excluded public benefit statute requires.

expectedJSON.body: California's default rule letting members remove a director without cause is worded differently, and is more freely displaceable, for a religious corporation than the corresponding default rule is for either a nonprofit public benefit corporation or a nonprofit mutual benefit corporation. The religious-corporation statute provides: “Except as provided in the articles or bylaws and subject to subdivision (b) of this section, any or all directors may be removed without cause if the removal is approved by the members.” The opening qualifier — “Except as provided in the articles or bylaws” — gives a religious corporation's own governing documents a general power to displace or modify this default in whatever way they choose. The corresponding public benefit corporation statute states the same basic default — members may remove a director without cause — but opens instead with “Subject to subdivisions (b) and (f) of this section,” not with any general “except as provided in the articles or bylaws” carve-out; its only built-in flexibility is the specific cumulative-voting protection in subdivision (b) and the specific designator-consent mechanism in subdivision (f), not a general license for the articles or bylaws to override the members' removal power itself. The nonprofit mutual benefit corporation's parallel removal statute is worded the same restrictive way as the public benefit corporation's. On this specific point — whether the corporation's own articles or bylaws may override the members' statutory power to remove a director without cause — the religious-corporation statute is the only one of the three that says so in its own opening text.

expectedJSON.body: The same point already made in this project's Nonprofit Public Benefit Corporation and Nonprofit Mutual Benefit Corporation documents applies here without needing to be re-derived: California's formation statute for a religious corporation — including the required purpose statement covered above — governs only what must appear in the articles filed with the California Secretary of State, and does not itself confer, guarantee, or evaluate federal tax-exempt status, which is a separate determination made by the Internal Revenue Service under federal law. One detail is specific to a religious corporation, however: the federal statute those other two documents already identify as the source of the 501(c)(3) organizational test lists “religious” purposes by name, on equal footing with “charitable,” “scientific,” and “educational” purposes, as one of the purposes for which a corporation must be “organized and operated exclusively” to qualify for exemption under 26 U.S.C. § 501(c)(3). That federal statutory alignment between the word “religious” in California's own formation statute and the word “religious” in the federal exemption statute does not collapse the two determinations into one — satisfying California's state-law purpose statement is still not the same thing as satisfying the IRS's separate organizational and operational tests under federal law, for the same reasons already given in this project's other two nonprofit corporation documents.
